chief_complaint: difficulty falling asleep taking 2 hours, daytime fatigue
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents with more than 3 months of difficulty falling asleep for about 2 hours on most nights and daytime fatigue, with symptoms gradually worsening.
ideas: He thinks looking at his phone in bed and drinking coffee late at the office has completely ruined his body's natural sleep cycle.
concerns: He is worried that being so exhausted during the day will lead to a costly mistake at work and cost him his job.
expectations: He hopes to get a prescription for a sleeping pill to knock him out and reset his sleep schedule.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Chronic Insomnia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Chronic insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity and circumstances, with daytime impairment, occurring at least three nights weekly for at least three months; assess for comorbid sleep, medical, substance, and psychiatric disorders.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: difficulty falling asleep taking 2 hours, daytime fatigue
Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents with more than 3 months of difficulty falling asleep for about 2 hours on most nights and daytime fatigue, with symptoms gradually worsening.

Objective/Exam findings: Obtain vital signs, BMI and focused cardiopulmonary/neurologic examination when indicated; assess daytime sleepiness and driving/occupational risk, mood, mania, psychosis, and suicide/self-harm risk. Use a sleep diary; arrange sleep testing when obstructive sleep apnea or another sleep disorder is suspected.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Insomnia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adjustment disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.

Missing suicidal ideation, severe depression, mania, psychosis, intoxication/withdrawal, delirium, or dangerous daytime sleepiness that needs urgent assessment or immediate driving/work-safety advice.
Treating insomnia solely with sedatives before identifying sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome, circadian disorder, pain, medications, caffeine/stimulants, alcohol, or psychiatric causes.
Using sedative-hypnotics without evaluating substance-use risk, interactions, next-day impairment, falls, dependence, and a time-limited plan.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Acute suicidal or homicidal ideation.
management_principles: Use CBT-I as first-line treatment, supported by a sleep diary and a consistent wake time, stimulus control, sleep restriction only when clinically appropriate, and reduction of late caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, and screens.
Treat identified contributors and refer for sleep evaluation when apnea, parasomnia, restless legs syndrome, circadian disorder, or marked daytime sleepiness is suspected.

Advise against driving or hazardous work when dangerously sleepy. Escalate urgently for suicide/self-harm/violence risk, mania, psychosis, delirium, or intoxication/withdrawal; if medication is used, choose it cautiously with monitoring and a limited duration.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 29-year-old man with more than three months of sleep-onset delay of about two hours on most nights and daytime fatigue. Confirm adequate sleep opportunity, frequency of at least three nights weekly, functional impact, sleep schedule, substances/medications, and symptoms of apnea, restless legs syndrome, circadian disorder, pain, mood disorder, mania, and trauma.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain vital signs, BMI and focused examination as indicated; assess daytime sleepiness and driving/work safety, mental status, and suicide, self-harm, violence, mania, psychosis, intoxication/withdrawal, and delirium. Use a sleep diary and obtain sleep testing when clinically indicated.
reference_soap.assessment: Probable chronic insomnia disorder if adequate sleep opportunity, frequency, daytime impairment, and exclusion criteria are confirmed; evaluate for comorbid sleep, psychiatric, medical, and substance-related causes.
reference_soap.plan: Start CBT-I and individualized behavioral sleep interventions with a sleep diary. Address contributors and refer for sleep evaluation when indicated. Give immediate driving/hazardous-work precautions for significant sleepiness and urgent escalation for acute safety risk, mania, psychosis, delirium, or substance withdrawal. Avoid routine long-term sedatives; if a medicine is considered, review interactions, misuse/dependence, and next-day impairment and monitor closely.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Chronic Insomnia
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Chronic Insomnia
Implement evidence-based management plan: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I)

teaching.one_liner: Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity, at least three nights weekly for at least three months, causing daytime impairment and not better explained by another disorder or substance.

must_ask.say: How long does it take you to fall asleep, and do you wake up during the night?
What do you do while lying awake — worry, use your phone, or just try to rest?
How is your concentration and mood during the day because of poor sleep?
Do you drink caffeine or alcohol, especially in the evening?
Do you snore, or feel like your legs are restless at night?

must_ask.objective: Daytime safety and urgent psychiatric symptoms
must_ask.say: Have you nodded off while driving or working, had thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else, or felt unusually energized with little need for sleep?

history.answer: I have been having a really hard time falling asleep for the past few months, and it leaves me exhausted during the day.
It takes me about two hours just to fall asleep once I lie down, but once I finally drift off, I usually sleep through until morning.
It started about three and a half months ago, and it happens almost every night, around five to six nights a week.
It started around the time I took on a stressful new project at work, but the sleep problem continued even after the project wrapped up.
I get into bed around eleven at night and wake up at seven in the morning, and my schedule stays the same on weekends.
I feel sluggish and fatigued throughout the day, and my concentration at work has noticeably declined.
I do feel drowsy during my drive home from work, and I had to pull over once because I caught myself nodding off.
When I cannot fall asleep, I keep watching the clock and scrolling on my phone, worrying about how tired I will be the next day.
I do not take naps during the day because I worry that napping will make it even harder to fall asleep at night.
I drink two cups of black coffee in the morning to stay awake, but I always stop drinking caffeine before noon.
I have a beer or two socially on weekends, but I never drink alcohol to help myself fall asleep.
No, I do not snore, and nobody has ever told me that I stop breathing or choke in my sleep.
No, my legs feel completely normal at night without any crawling sensations or urge to move them.
I work standard daytime office hours from nine to six and have never done shift work or night shifts.
I feel stressed and anxious specifically about not sleeping, but I do not feel depressed or hopeless about my life.
No, I have never had any thoughts of hurting myself or wishing I were dead.
No, I have never experienced periods where I felt energetic or euphoric despite barely sleeping.
I do not have any chest pain, heartburn, cough, shortness of breath, or need to urinate during the night.
I tried an over-the-counter herbal sleep tea a month ago with no success, and I have not taken any prescription sleeping pills.
My bedroom is quiet, dark, and kept at a comfortable temperature, and I sleep alone in my room.
I thought maybe all the late-night screen time and caffeine at work just completely threw off my sleep rhythm.
I'm really worried that this constant exhaustion will cause me to mess up on the job and get fired.
I'm hoping you can prescribe me some sleeping pills so I can finally get a full night of rest and reset my routine.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any regular prescription medications or dietary supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I work as a software engineer at a technology company and live alone in an apartment.
Both of my parents are healthy, and no one in my family has a history of sleep disorders or mental health conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, mildly tired-appearing young male with normal body habitus, body mass index 22.8 kg/m2, and normal neck circumference without crowded features.
Alert and fully oriented; speech is fluent and coherent; affect is mildly anxious regarding sleep but congruent, with no thought disorder, delusions, or suicidal ideation.
Oropharynx is clear with normal tonsils, no mucosal erythema, and Mallampati class I airway without posterior pharyngeal crowding.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and smooth with no palpable nodules or thyromegaly.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes or crackles.
